lessons.title: Zero to ten
lessons.goal: Count from 0 to 10 and catch a number.

tip.title: Two ways to say cinco
tip.body: In most of Spain, c before e/i and z sound like the th in "think": cinco is "THEEN-ko". In Latin America, the Canary Islands and parts of Andalusia they sound like s: "SEEN-ko". Both are correct, so pick one and be consistent. Uno becomes un before a masculine noun (un café) and una before a feminine one (una cerveza).

phrases.note: Numbers are masculine: el siete, el nueve.

lessons.title: Eleven to twenty & your age
lessons.goal: Count to 20 and say how old you are.

tip.title: You "have" your age
tip.body: Spanish uses tener (to have) for age: Tengo veinte años, literally "I have twenty years". Never say soy veinte. Eleven to fifteen are special words (once, doce, trece, catorce, quince); from sixteen they're built as "ten and six" and written as one word: dieciséis, diecisiete, dieciocho, diecinueve.

phrases.note: Asking adults their age can be a bit personal, just as in English.

lines.n: Happy birthday! How old are you?

prompts.n: Ask a friend how old they are.

lessons.title: Up to 100 & phone numbers
lessons.goal: Say any number to 100 and give your phone number.

tip.title: veintiuno, but treinta y uno
tip.body: 21 to 29 are one word: veintiuno, veintidós, veintitrés… From 31 you add y ("and"): treinta y uno, cuarenta y cinco, noventa y nueve. Exactly 100 is cien. Phone numbers are usually read in small groups, often pairs: 45 is cuarenta y cinco, not cuatro, cinco.

lessons.title: tener: tengo, tienes, tiene…
lessons.goal: Say what you have and how old people are.

tip.title: tener is irregular
tip.body: yo tengo, tú tienes, usted/él/ella tiene, nosotros tenemos, vosotros tenéis (Spain), ustedes/ellos tienen. The e turns into ie in tienes, tiene and tienen, and the yo form is tengo. Plural nouns add -s after a vowel (hermano → hermanos) and -es after a consonant (un mes → dos meses). A mixed group of brothers and sisters is hermanos.

phrases.t: Tenemos un perro y dos gatos.
phrases.n: We have a dog and two cats.

lessons.title: My numbers
lessons.goal: Talk about your name, age, family and phone number for 45 seconds.

culture.title: Two surnames
culture.body: In Spain and most of Latin America, people have two surnames: traditionally the father's first surname followed by the mother's first surname. In the writer Gabriel García Márquez, García comes from his father and Márquez from his mother, so he is "García Márquez", not "Márquez". In everyday life many people use only the first surname, but both appear on official documents. In Spain, women keep their own surnames when they marry, and parents can now choose the order of their children's surnames.

free.n: Talk about your numbers: your name and surname, your age, how many brothers and sisters you have and your phone number.
